title: CMMC Phase 2: Current Policy and Contractor Readiness
summary: CMMC Phase 2: Current Policy and Contractor Readiness: scope, evidence, limitations, and the decisions buyers need to make.
body_markdown:
## Which obligations should contractors continue addressing?


Continue addressing the safeguarding, assessment, reporting, and flow-down duties actually included in the contract. A pause in a rollout milestone is not permission to misrepresent implemented controls.


[DFARS 252.204-7012](https://www.acquisition.gov/dfars/252.204-7012-safeguarding-covered-defense-information-and-cyber-incident-reporting.) addresses covered defense information, safeguarding, and cyber incident reporting. Identify the information you receive or create, where it flows, and the service providers that can access it. Record the contractual basis for your system boundary.


Which obligations should contractors continue addressing? — comparison Decision Evidence to keep


Which information is in scope? Contract language, agency designation, authorized CUI categories


Which systems handle it? Inventory and data-flow diagram


Which assessment status is required? Solicitation, amendments, clauses, written clarification


Which controls operate? System security plan and reviewable evidence


Which gaps remain? Accurate remediation ownership and status


## What should be ready before a C3PAO engagement?


A defensible scope, accurate system security plan, implemented controls, and accessible evidence should precede scheduling. Verify the organization’s current directory role and standing in the[Cyber AB Marketplace](https://cyberab.org/Catalog) , then discuss assessment scope, conflicts, team availability, and terms.


Use the[C3PAO selection guide](https://blog.getagency.com/articles/cmmc-c3pao-list) for the diligence questions. Do not buy an assessment solely because an old deadline appears in a blog or sales presentation.


## How should you maintain the readiness plan while policy changes?


Keep the underlying control work moving while updating the source of each external deadline. Track current policy, written contract requirements, remediation, and assessment scheduling as separate items.


Assign one owner to review official updates and communicate changes to procurement, engineering, and leadership. Keep dated evidence of the decision, including what changed and why. That provides a usable plan even when an implementation schedule changes.
